title: How Many Kinds of Soldiery There Are, and Concerning Mercenaries
hook: The velvet pay purse shines above the ditch where hired horsemen will not stand.
counterintuition: The mistake is to treat mercenaries as ready-made strength. Hired arms can look brave in display, but their stipend, discipline, courage, and ambition are not bound to the state that needs them to die.
tryThisNow: Choose one paid force from history. Write who paid it, which hardship it avoided, and whether its captain became dangerous by skill or by failure.
keyTakeaway: Good arms must belong to the state; mercenaries make a weak foundation because their pay, courage, discipline, and captains answer to a separate interest.

breakdown.fastRead: A senator sees a velvet pay purse hang from a saddle horn while hired horsemen wait outside the muddy infantry ditch. The senate war order says they are the republic's army. The ditch says otherwise. They are paid to appear, not rooted enough to suffer for the state. Good laws need good arms under them, and hired arms leave both shaky. If the captain is weak, he loses for you. If he is strong, he may use victory against you.
breakdown.deepRead:
A lagoon republic can hire a famous mounted company faster than it can train its own infantry. The horses look clean. The captain bows. The pay chest closes with a public click. Yet when mud, night, or winter asks for hardship, the hired force begins to show its true owner. Its reason for staying is stipend, and stipend is too thin a cause for dying.

Good arms are one of the foundations of every state. Laws cannot stand well where arms do not stand for the state itself. Mercenaries break that foundation because they are disunited, ambitious, without discipline, and faithful only while danger stays away. They can rob in peace and run in war. Destruction is delayed only until a real enemy arrives.

A coastal queen points to the snow tide and orders a winter strike on a raider camp. The crossbow captain taps the winter clause in his contract and leaves the night ladders by the fire. This is not just bad mood or bad weather. Mercenary rules are written to spare fatigue and danger: no night attack, no winter campaign, no stockade, no ditch, no hard infantry work.

The captain creates a second danger. If he is unskillful, the state is ruined in the ordinary way. If he is skillful, he becomes a threat through his own ambition. Sforza, Carmignuola, Vaila, and Italy's ruin all press the same point: a prince or republic that rests on hired arms owns the bill, not the army.
breakdown.fullRead:
A wet bridge pennon drips beside an enemy duke's wax offer in the hill council chamber. Maura reconstructs the morning after the hired captain took the bridge. The city bells had barely stopped when his clerk placed the duke's offer on top of the republic's pay schedule. The victory did not make the republic safe. It gave the captain a market.

Look under the city laws and ask what arms hold them up. A ruler who has laws without arms that answer to the state is building on borrowed ground. Mercenaries look like a shortcut because they already know drill, horses, ransom custom, and the names of enemy captains. The shortcut hides the fatal split. Their body is in your field, but their interest is not the state's interest.

In the quiet months, a hired force may seem useful. It can parade, escort officials, threaten small towns, and look valiant among friends. The trouble begins when an enemy asks it to pay the full price of defense. A trifle of stipend does not make men willing to die for you. When danger arrives, the soldier can run, bargain, delay, or preserve the market that feeds him.

A city league shows the market at work. Magistrate Radu predicts a dawn attack on the enemy camp. Instead he sees cavalry chalk ransom marks on prisoners while the enemy stockade stands untouched. Captured men can be traded. A broken camp ends work. The league's money buys motion, honor, and prisoners, but not the thing the state needs: the enemy's force destroyed.

At the captain's table, the trap has two sides. A bad captain ruins the employer through incompetence. A good captain can ruin him through power. If the captain wins, he may bargain with the enemy, oppress his employer, or turn his soldiers toward a private rise. The employer cannot relax either way. Weakness loses the war; skill may steal the victory.

In Italy's hired camps, the military pattern made the political danger worse. Mercenary leaders lowered the credit of infantry because infantry was expensive to keep and gave less honor to mounted captains. Cavalry made them visible and payable. So armies became bright in horsemen and thin in foot soldiers. They avoided fatigue and danger by custom: no winter campaigns, no night attacks, no hard camp works with stockade or ditch. They fought in a way that protected their trade until foreign armies showed the hollowness.

A river duke learns it late. Before the foreign infantry crosses, Rostan admires polished lance pennants over an empty citizen pike rack. After the first drumline, the pennants lie in the reeds. The laws of his duchy still exist on paper, but the arms beneath them have scattered. Good arms are not decoration for the state. They are the force that keeps law from becoming a request.

Use the warning with care. This is not a claim that every paid soldier is worthless in every task. It is a warning against making hired arms the foundation of rule. A republic may pay specialists, scouts, or engineers. A prince may use wages inside an army that remains his own. But when the captain, discipline, courage, and rules of danger belong to a separate company, the state has confused a contract with command. A clay recall tablet cannot bind a private drum.

examples.title: Vero Watches the Horsemen Avoid the Ditch

planSpec.domain: a lagoon republic hiring a mounted condottiere company for its first mainland campaign
planSpec.audience: senators who mistake the captain's display for a state foundation
planSpec.stakes: if the captain wins he can bargain against them, and if he hesitates the republic has no infantry of its own to hold the field
planSpec.requiredBeat: The captain bows beside his pay purse, then keeps his horsemen outside the muddy infantry ditch while the senators notice the field is being defended by men who own no part of it.

examples.scenario: A velvet pay purse hangs from a saddle horn above a muddy infantry ditch outside the lagoon camp at 6:20 a.m. Senator Vero carries the senate war order to the mounted condottiere captain and must decide whether this display is a foundation. The captain bows beside his purse, then keeps his horsemen outside the ditch while Vero notices the field is defended by men who own no part of it.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the display as hired motion, not a state foundation. Vero should count the republic's own infantry and command before trusting the mounted company with the field.
examples.whyItMatters: The captain's pay binds him to a contract, not to the republic's survival. Without owned foot soldiers, the state has no force left if he hesitates or bargains.

examples.title: Maura Finds the Duke's Offer

planSpec.domain: a hill republic whose hired captain captures a bridge and immediately negotiates with the enemy duke
planSpec.audience: a council that thought a capable mercenary was safer than training citizens
planSpec.stakes: the very skill that won the bridge now gives the captain leverage to oppress his employer or sell the victory elsewhere
planSpec.requiredBeat: The council messenger finds the bridge pennon still wet, but the captain has placed the enemy duke's wax offer on top of the republic's pay schedule.

examples.scenario: A wet bridge pennon drips beside an enemy duke's wax offer in the hill republic's council chamber at 9:10 a.m. Maura, the council messenger, writes the postmortem after the hired captain's victory. She finds the pennon still wet, but the captain has placed the duke's wax offer on top of the republic's pay schedule.
examples.whatToDo: Read the victory as leverage. Maura should report that the captain's skill has made him dangerous because he can now sell the bridge or force better terms.
examples.whyItMatters: A capable mercenary can threaten the employer after success. The bridge gives him bargaining power because the republic did not train citizens to hold it.

examples.title: Beatrix Points to the Snow Tide

planSpec.domain: a coastal queen hiring crossbow companies who refuse a winter assault on a raider camp
planSpec.audience: a queen learning why stipend soldiers avoid the exact hardship the state requires
planSpec.stakes: the raiders will return if the camp is not struck in winter, but the hired companies have written their rules to avoid cold, night, and danger
planSpec.requiredBeat: When she points to the snow tide, the captain taps the winter clause in his contract and leaves the night ladders stacked by the fire.

examples.scenario: Night ladders lean by a fire beside a contract winter clause in the coastal queen's war tent at 11:45 p.m. "The snow tide will cover our approach," Queen Beatrix says, pointing to the marker. Captain Osric taps the winter clause. "Not in this season." He leaves the night ladders stacked by the fire while Beatrix must decide what her stipend has truly bought.
examples.whatToDo: Judge the companies by the hardship they refuse. Beatrix should see that paid crossbows are avoiding the winter night assault the kingdom actually needs.
examples.whyItMatters: The raider camp survives if the hard strike is skipped. A contract written to avoid cold, night, and danger protects the company before it protects the coast.

examples.title: Radu Sees the Stockade Untouched

planSpec.domain: a city league paying a cavalry band that keeps taking prisoners instead of breaking enemy camps
planSpec.audience: magistrates wondering why campaigns look honorable and produce no security
planSpec.stakes: prisoner exchanges preserve the mercenary market, while enemy camps and towns remain intact
planSpec.requiredBeat: The magistrate predicts the dawn camp attack, then watches the cavalry captain chalk ransom marks on prisoners while the enemy stockade stands untouched.

examples.scenario: Ransom chalk marks cover prisoners' sleeves below an untouched stockade outside the city league camp at dawn. Magistrate Radu predicts that the cavalry band will break the enemy camp after yesterday's order. Then he watches the captain chalk ransom marks on prisoners while the enemy stockade stands untouched. Radu must decide whether this honorable campaign has produced security.
examples.whatToDo: Measure the campaign by enemy capacity destroyed. Radu should mark prisoner-taking as mercenary market work, not as defense of the city league.
examples.whyItMatters: Ransoms preserve the trade that feeds the cavalry band. The enemy camp remains able to fight, so the league pays for motion without gaining safety.

examples.title: Rostan Finds the Pike Rack Empty

planSpec.domain: a river duchy replacing citizen pikes with a famous hired lance school
planSpec.audience: a duke comparing parade brilliance with actual defense when foreign infantry arrives
planSpec.stakes: the hired lances look valiant among friends but scatter before disciplined infantry, leaving laws without arms beneath them
planSpec.requiredBeat: Before the foreign infantry crosses, the duke admires polished lance pennants; after the first drumline, those pennants lie in the reeds while the old citizen pike rack is empty.

examples.scenario: Polished lance pennants shine above an empty citizen pike rack in Arno Gate's west armoury yard at 12:00 p.m. Before the foreign infantry crosses the river, Rostan, ruling duke of the river duchy, admires the hired lance school's parade line. After the first drumline, those pennants lie in the reeds while the old citizen pike rack is empty. Rostan must decide what defense his laws really had beneath them.
examples.whatToDo: Compare parade arms with battle arms. Rostan should rebuild citizen infantry instead of mistaking hired lance brilliance for the force that keeps law standing.
examples.whyItMatters: The lances were brave among friends and brittle before disciplined infantry. With the pike rack empty, the duchy's laws have no owned arms under them.

examples.title: Ines Hears the Recall Tablet Read

planSpec.domain: a republic recalling a failing hired general but discovering no law can bind his private company
planSpec.audience: lawmakers who confused paying a captain with commanding an army
planSpec.stakes: citizen captains can be recalled by law, but a mercenary head leaves with the force or turns it against the state
planSpec.requiredBeat: The recall tablet is read aloud, and the hired general lifts his private company drum from the assembly floor before any soldier obeys the republic's clerk.

examples.scenario: A private company drum sits in front of a clay recall tablet on the republic assembly floor at 4:30 p.m. Clerk Ines must decide whether reading the law will command the failing hired general. She reads the recall tablet aloud. Before any soldier obeys the republic's clerk, the general lifts his private company drum and the company turns toward the door.
examples.whatToDo: Distinguish payment from command. Ines should report that the republic can recall a citizen captain by law, but this private company follows its own drum.
examples.whyItMatters: A state that pays a force does not necessarily command it. If the army belongs to the captain, recall law may leave with him instead of binding him.

questions.prompt: A republic hires a mounted company for a mainland campaign. The captain looks splendid in camp, but his men refuse to enter the muddy infantry ditch. What should the senate see?
choices: A foundation for law because the company is already trained.
A hired display that leaves the republic without owned arms where hardship begins.
A harmless delay because cavalry should never work near infantry.
questions.explanation: The ditch exposes the missing foundation. Training and display do not matter if the force is paid to appear but not bound to suffer where the state needs it.

questions.prompt: A mercenary captain captures a bridge, then places the enemy duke's offer on top of the city pay schedule. Why is the captain now dangerous?
choices: His skill gives him leverage to bargain against the city that hired him.
His victory proves hired arms are always safer than citizen arms.
The bridge no longer matters because the battle has already been won.
questions.explanation: A capable hired captain can become dangerous through success. The bridge gives him something to sell, while the city lacks its own force to hold the gain.

questions.prompt: A queen orders a winter night strike on a raider camp. The hired crossbow captain points to a contract clause against winter operations and leaves the ladders by the fire. What has failed?
choices: The queen failed because winter attacks are never useful.
The ladders failed because crossbow companies should fight only at sea.
The hired force's rules avoid the exact danger the state must face.
questions.explanation: The issue is not weather alone. The raider camp must be struck now, but the company has written its service to avoid cold, night, and danger.

questions.prompt: A city league pays cavalry to break enemy camps. After each skirmish, the cavalry marks prisoners for ransom while the stockades remain untouched. What is the structural problem?
choices: The cavalry is preserving its market instead of destroying the enemy's capacity.
The league is wrong to care whether enemy stockades remain.
Ransom marks prove the campaign is producing enough security.
questions.explanation: Prisoners can be exchanged and sold, so the mercenary trade continues. The untouched stockade shows the enemy's force remains intact.

questions.prompt: A duchy replaces citizen pikes with hired lances. The lances shine in parade, then scatter when foreign infantry drums cross the river. What did the duke misunderstand?
choices: Parade brilliance and mounted reputation are not the same as owned arms that can meet disciplined infantry.
Foreign infantry can always defeat every kind of army.
Citizen pikes are useful only for ceremonies.
questions.explanation: The duke mistook display for a foundation. Hired lances looked valiant among friends, but the empty pike rack left the state without its own infantry.

questions.prompt: A republic reads a recall order to a failing hired general. He lifts his private company drum, and the soldiers leave with him before the clerk finishes. What should lawmakers learn?
choices: A law that recalls a captain is useless in every republic.
Paying a captain is not the same as commanding the force he owns.
The clerk should have read the order in a louder voice.
questions.explanation: Citizen captains can be held by civic law; a private company follows the captain's drum. The republic confused a payroll with command.

questions.prompt: At a border muster, a prince keeps a dull mercenary captain because the man seems too unskilled to become ambitious. The hired company will face a real enemy at dawn. Which judgment is sound?
choices: An unskillful captain is safe because he cannot become ambitious.
The captain's skill level does not matter once he is paid.
An unskillful captain still ruins the prince in the ordinary way by losing.
questions.explanation: Skill and lack of skill create different dangers. The able captain may oppress the employer; the incapable one loses the war and ruins him by failure.

questions.prompt: A hired army has many horsemen, few infantry, no winter campaigns, no night attacks, and no stockade or ditch around camp. What does this pattern show?
choices: A professional code that makes the army more reliable in danger.
A set of habits designed to reduce fatigue and risk for the mercenary company.
A clever way to make citizen infantry unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The pattern matches the mechanics of mercenary weakness. Cavalry display and rules against hard work protect the company, not the state.

questions.prompt: A city has detailed laws and a famous hired army, but no citizens trained to fight and no prince commanding in person. What is the best judgment?
choices: The laws are secure because hired soldiers are specialists.
The city has good laws but lacks the good arms needed to support them.
The hired army is safe as long as the city pays on time.
questions.explanation: Good laws need arms that answer to the state. A famous hired force may parade well, but payment alone does not bind courage, discipline, or command.

reviewCards.front: A republic has laws and hired soldiers but no owned army. What foundation is missing?
reviewCards.back: Good arms are missing. Laws stand poorly when the force beneath them is paid to serve but not rooted in the state.

reviewCards.front: A mercenary captain is very capable. Why can that be worse than simple weakness?
reviewCards.back: A capable captain can use victory as leverage, bargain with enemies, or turn the army toward private ambition. An incapable one ruins you by losing.

reviewCards.front: Hired soldiers are brave in camp but hesitate before real danger. What does the stipend fail to buy?
reviewCards.back: A stipend may buy service while danger is light, but it does not bind soldiers to die for a state they do not own or command.

reviewCards.front: No winter campaign, no night attack, no stockade, no ditch. What are these rules protecting?
reviewCards.back: They protect the mercenary company from fatigue and danger. They do not protect the state that needs hard work when enemies arrive.

reviewCards.front: Why does a hired cavalry band with few foot soldiers worry Machiavelli's test?
reviewCards.back: Cavalry display gives captains honor and pay, but thin infantry leaves the state weak against disciplined enemies and unable to hold ground.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Test whether arms belong to the state or merely stand near it for pay. Look past display and ask who commands the force, what danger it avoids, and whether success gives its captain leverage against the employer.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a state relies on a paid company, then identify what hardship the contract lets it avoid and what force remains if it refuses.
If a hired captain wins a major objective, then ask what he can now bargain for and whether the employer has owned troops to hold the gain.
If cavalry, uniforms, or reputation dominate the display, then inspect infantry, camp works, winter readiness, and night operations.
If a republic tries to remove a hired commander, then ask whether soldiers obey civic law or the captain's private drum.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one paid army from history and write three lines: who paid it, which danger it avoided, and how its captain's skill or failure threatened the employer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, read one campaign account involving hired soldiers. Mark each force as owned, mercenary, auxiliary, or mixed, then note who controlled the captain when danger rose.

memorableLines.text: If the captain is weak, he loses for you.
memorableLines.why: It gives the first half of the captain danger in plain words.

memorableLines.text: If he is strong, he may use victory against you.
memorableLines.why: It completes the trap: competence can be dangerous when arms are not owned.

memorableLines.text: A clay recall tablet cannot bind a private drum.
memorableLines.why: It turns the command-versus-contract problem into a concrete image.
